craft_claim: A narrator's deliberate disclosure of private emotional interiority (not mere factual report) increases reader liking and felt closeness toward the narrator.

supporting_evidence.location: Psychological Bulletin 116(3): 457-475, abstract and meta-analytic results
supporting_evidence.note: Meta-analysis finds that people who engage in intimate disclosures are liked more than people who disclose at lower levels, and that people come to like others as a result of having disclosed to them.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 74(5): 1238-1251, Study 2
supporting_evidence.note: Self-disclosure of emotion predicts experienced intimacy more strongly than self-disclosure of facts and information.

supporting_evidence.location: Chapters on breadth and depth of exchange and the social penetration process
supporting_evidence.note: Closeness develops through graduated increases in the breadth and depth of self-disclosure; disclosure is the mechanism of relational penetration.

scope: Narrator-to-reader address in prose, memoir, essay, and copy where interiority is disclosed rather than described from outside.
exceptions: Disclosure that violates audience or role expectations can reduce liking rather than increase it; see clm-tone-intimate-disclosure-risk-boundaries.
